answers: Two workers at a Chicago day care were fired and arrested after a disturbing incident that left five toddlers injured. Police say surveillance video captured one of the workers burning the 2-year-olds with a hot glue gun while the other woman watched and laughed, People reports. Lizandra Cosme, 32, has been charged with five counts of aggravated battery of a child causing great bodily harm, the Chicago Sun-Times reports. Susana Gonzalez, 27, faces five misdemeanor charges of causing the circumstances of child endangerment over the Dec. 1 incident at the Children's Place day care. It's not clear how seriously the children were injured. Prosecutors say Cosme, who brought the glue gun for a Christmas project, was captured on video applying the hot glue directly to the hands and arms of the three girls and two boys. "Each of the child victims winced and some whined at the hot glue gun application," a prosecutor said during a Monday court appearance. Prosecutors said Cosme tried to cover up the incident, asking a father whether his child had been burned at home, ABC7 reports. They said her actions were discovered when one child's mother, an ER physician, saw the burns and demanded to see surveillance footage. Cosme's lawyer said his client "screwed up" but did not mean to hurt the children.

full.prediction:
**Summary of News:**

Two daycare workers, Lizandra Cosme, 32, and Susana Gonzalez, 27, have been charged following an incident in which five toddlers were injured with a hot glue gun at the Children’s Learning Place daycare in Chicago. The incident occurred on December 1, 2024, and was captured on surveillance footage, which reportedly showed Cosme applying hot glue to the hands and arms of five 2-year-old children, causing them to wince and cry in pain. Gonzalez, who was present in the room, is alleged to have laughed as the incident unfolded.

Cosme, who was working with 16 children at the time, is accused of five felony counts of aggravated battery to a child, while Gonzalez faces five misdemeanor charges of child endangerment. Cosme was denied bail during her court appearance and is scheduled to return to court on December 26. Her defense attorney stated that Cosme’s actions were not malicious, though she admitted to “screwing up” during the incident.

According to prosecutors, Cosme brought the hot glue gun from home to the daycare for a Christmas project. The incident was reportedly discovered when the mother of one of the children, an emergency room physician, noticed the burns and requested a review of the surveillance footage. Cosme allegedly attempted to cover up the incident by asking the father of one of the children if the child had been injured at home.

The daycare center, which serves children from 6 weeks to 6 years old, immediately terminated both Cosme and Gonzalez following the alleged incident. In a statement, the daycare’s spokeswoman, Lissa Druss Christman, emphasized the importance of the children’s well-being and noted that the facility had notified the Department of Children and Family Services (DCFS) and is cooperating with the investigation.

The DCFS is currently investigating the allegations of abuse and child endangerment. The incident has sparked public outrage and raised concerns about child safety in daycare settings. The case highlights the serious consequences of negligence and the importance of strict oversight in childcare facilities.
